speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. E. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MESSAGE OF LOYALTY AND DEVOTION ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, May 24, Her Majesty's birthday is officially celebrated. It is fitting, I think, that this day should also have been designated Commonwealth Day. Her Majesty is now head of a Commonwealth which includes 21 countries in every part of the world. On Her Majesty's birthday, which is also Commonwealth Day, the Royal Union flag, the Union Jack, will be flying on Parliament Hill alongside the new flag of Canada for the first time.
As we will not be sitting on Monday I believe it is fitting to propose, and I hope the Leader of the Official Opposition will be good enough to second my proposal, that you, Mr. Speaker, should convey to Her Majesty the loyal and affectionate congratulations of this House on her birthday. It seems to me that the deep feelings of admiration and respect which the Canadian people have for our wise and gracious Sovereign would be fittingly reflected in such a message.
Our association with Great Britain, Mr. Speaker, through the Commonwealth and through the Crown represents the continuity of our history and the depths of our roots. The Crown is also an integral part of our Parliamentary system and one which it is important for us to maintain and respect as we face the problems and the opportunities of the future.
In this spirit, Mr. Speaker, we wish Her Majesty all the best of health and happiness for many, many years, and we send her our warmest birthday greetings.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MESSAGE OF LOYALTY AND DEVOTION ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to join with the Prime Minister in this message of loyalty and devotion to the Queen on the anniversary of her birthday. As I listened to the Prime Minister it occurred to me it is of significance that we have at the present time in the City of Ottawa representatives of
the United States Congress from the Senate and the House of Representatives.
The Prime Minister spoke of the Commonwealth. The concept of the Commonwealth was first formulated in 1775. After the battles of Concord and Bunker Hill representatives of the 13 colonies joined together in a petition known as the olive branch petition which Benjamin Franklin took to the United Kingdom and endeavoured to have the Crown of that day accept. That olive branch petition was signed by John Hancock and the other representatives of the 13 colonies who subsequently signed the Declaration of Independence. Had it been accepted the principles of the Commonwealth would have then seen their beginning. Everything that was ultimately placed in the Statute of Westminster of 1930 was included in the olive branch petition. Indeed, among the most dramatic things in history are the concluding words of that petition, where the 13 colonies stated "if only you will give us the right of self government as we ask we shall throughout the generations to come give loyalty and devotion to the British Crown".
Her Majesty performs an abiding function not only within the Commonwealth but also internationally. At this very moment in West Germany she, removed as she is from party politics and the divisions that sometimes separate us within the nation, is doing her part magnificently to bind the wounds of two world wars and to assure that for generations to come the things that have separated Britain and Germany will no longer exist. She is playing a part that I am sure will bear fruit.
I join with the Prime Minister, as I am sure all hon. Members do, in his eloquent words of loyalty which I know Your Honour will transmit to her.

We wish also to extend a hearty welcome to our visitors from the United States who are with us at this time. In a world which is strife torn and sadly divided we believe the Commonwealth has an important role to

It is not a tightly knit organization, but is a loose federation of many peoples, different tongues and different races, who are bound together by a loyalty to the common ideals which we cherish and which are symbolized by the Crown. It is therefore singularly fitting that on May 24 the Canadian Parliament and Canadian people should give thought to the two ideas contained in the celebration of that day, namely our faith in the role which the Commonwealth can play in world affairs and in the sentiment of loyalty which we extend to Her Majesty the Queen.
We in this group join with others in sending to Her Majesty our best wishes and our greetings on this her official birthday.

Mr. Speaker, it is not too long ago that we were greatly honoured to have a visit from Her Majesty. At that time and during the months that have passed, we have remembered with a great deal of pleasure the way in which Her Majesty moved among the people of Canada and enhanced the position of the Crown in our nation. I am sure that on this occasion when we are commemorating the birthday of Her Majesty, it is well that the Prime Minister should move this motion and that we would join with him, and with the other speakers, in expressing our sincere wishes that she will enjoy a great many years of health and real happiness.
Reference has been made this morning to the Commonwealth. We realize, of course, that the concept of the Commonwealth has changed drastically down through the years. We do believe that the Commonwealth still plays a very important part in international relations. I had the opportunity, along with other Members of this House to attend the meeting of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association conference last fall. We were reminded again that in spite of the fact there were so many diverse peoples there from all parts of the world, there was a unity of purpose, a common bond that united us. We want to see that strengthened and developed in the days that lie ahead.
So, Mr. Speaker, we in this party would like to associate ourselves with the message of greeting and best wishes that will be conveyed to Her Majesty.

I know all hon. Members wish to join me in the welcome you have extended to our visitors. We all greatly appreciate the fact that some of the most important and busiest members of Congress have found the time to come to Ottawa for this meeting, on the United States side under the leadership of Senator George Aiken of Vermont and Representative Cornelius E. Gallagher of New Jersey. Our welcome also expresses our warm appreciation of the work the joint Parliamentary committee is doing in the field of United States-Canadian relations.
This committee was set up, that is on the Canadian side, in the time of the right hon. gentleman the Leader of the Opposition when he was Prime Minister. It was one of his good deeds which we acknowledge. Our welcome is also a recognition of the significance we attach to the maintenance of United States-Canadian relations on the legislative side as well as on the executive level.
The problems between our two countries are, of course, many. Some are related to the burden of leadership in the world which the people of the United States are carrying with such courage and devotion in our efforts to secure peace and freedom. Others are bilateral in character arising out of our continental relationship. Whatever they are, our two countries seek to find solutions to these problems in a spirit of good will, good neighbourliness and understanding. The meetings of the joint parliamentary conference have increased that good will and understanding, and I am sure the present meeting will continue to do so.

For instance, as regards the first paragraph of motion No. 14, we know that there is an amendment and a subamendment to remove supplementary estimates from the 36-day period allocated to the business of supply. I wonder why they want to remove those estimates from that period. As far as I am concerned, I would have preferred the removal of interim supply voted on every month, because if a majority government is elected, and even with a minority government as we have today, it is often the only opportunity which the opposition has of automatically overthrowing the government by extending the debate on interim supply. In fact, I think this procedure may be necessary in some circumstances, particularly when the government goes beyond its rights and privileges.
If consideration of interim supply took the whole 36 days allocated-consideration of interim supply has often taken up to 15 days -then there would be no time left for consideration of the main estimates of every department.
That is why I think it would perhaps be better to reduce this 36 days period to 30 days and to remove consideration of interim supply from the time allocated for consideration of estimates in general.
However, since an amendment has been moved so that supplementary estimates will not be included, I feel that this is an improvement, even if the 36-day period for the general consideration of estimates has to be shortened. That is why we will support this proposal not to include supplementary estimates in the period of time provided by the first paragraph of motion No. 14.
Mr. Speaker, I think that this motion should also include provisions in the event the estimates of all departments would not have been considered in the 36-day period. Would the estimates not discussed be passed automatically? In the affirmative, I believe that this would be unfair, especially if some members wanted to deal rather extensively with a specific problem and did not leave enough time for other members to discuss other problems.
As far as the suggestion to sit during the supper hour is concerned, that is between six and eight o'clock, I do not feel that this would really expedite the business of the house.
Of course, we know that members would leave in turn to go and have supper, but we must take under consideration the fact that at the present time there are complaints to
1566	COMMONS

Since it seems there is practically unanimous objection to that suggestion to sit during the supper hour, I feel that the government might easily reverse its decision on that matter.
Mr. Speaker, another very important point in this motion is the one dealing with the abolition of the appeal against the Speaker's ruling. With all due respect, I think the house, which is the final authority as far as its business and decisions are concerned, as the Chair has stated many times, should keep its right and its privilege of appealing against the Speaker's rulings, particularly when some members are not pleased with them. At least, this would allow the house to vote on the merits of such and such ruling, and I am sure that in the long run it would prove wiser to maintain the right of appeal against the Speaker's rulings.
On the whole, we are in favour of improving the rules so as to have more time to legislate in the people's interest. We feel that time is being wasted in the house, that it would be advisable to shorten some debates in order to discuss more measures. I feel, however, that such motions are dangerous for the house as a whole, because they are not specific enough, and do not indicate exactly what is intended under the new changes in the standing orders. In my opinion, enough care has not been taken to safeguard the rights and privileges of the opposition, as well as of the third parties.
For instance, paragraph 2 of the new standing order 15A provides that after discussion with representatives of the various parties, if no agreement has been reached- and even though all opposition parties may object-about the allocation of time for consideration of some items of business, the minister concerned may then propose just the same that the debate on a piece of legislation be restricted. I think that this attitude would be unfair for the house as a whole and as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out yesterday, the government should reconsider the strict provisions of the proposed subsection 5 of section 15a. In addition, I feel some provisions of this section should be clarified and made more flexible.

Last year I attended the meetings of the committee on procedure set up to attempt to speed up the business of the house. A similar change to that proposed in subsection 2 of motion No. 14 was submitted and accepted. I had personally endorsed it, but it was much more flexible than the amendment now proposed.
If the government tries too hard to stifle the opposition-even the word "guillotine" was used, which seems to me to be a bit too strong for the time being-we can nevertheless find some means to prevent them from stifling us too long. Besides, what is the meaning of "guillotine"? It means nothing more nor less than "to kill", "to decapitate", and this is out of the question.
However, if the government seeks to stifle the opposition, then the image of this house and of the parliament of the nation will become tarnished.
Mr. Speaker, before I conclude my remarks, I would like to add one more thing.
There are, in this house, interpreters, reporters, civil servants working on Hansard, in short all the regular staff of the house of Commons.
If the hours of sitting are increased, it seems to me that it would be necessary to increase also the staff who already have to work late at night very often. The work done by those employees is often extremely tiring. Take for instance the case of the simultaneous translators. They spend most of the day in little cubicles where they must not always be comfortable; moreover, their work is extremely difficult because it requires their unwavering attention, especially when the speakers talk quickly, when there are interruptions, and so on.
The reporters find themselves in the same situation. They must do tiring, nerve-wracking work. In my opinion, the government must -and it is morally obligated to-increase considerably the present staff of the House of Commons because these people have a difficult task to do.
Those employees have to follow the proceedings continually. I also think that their salary should be raised because those are jobs where there is no set time and the number of hours will increase further because we may sit at night even later than we do at the present time, and even during the lunch hour. Furthermore, Hansard employees have to go on working after the house has adjourned.
May 21, 19G5

Mr. Speaker, 1 think everybody will recognize that there is an urgent need to increase the personnel and their salaries.
Take for instance the French debates section; it has a smaller staff than the English side. This means that they have more work to do. It is not that I would like to cut the personnel of the English debates-I think they also need to be increased-but I insist on the fact that the French debates personnel must be increased because they have to do the same job as the English section, with fewer people.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this suggestion should be taken into serious consideration by the government because that is an urgent need.
In conclusion, I should like to say-and on this I will put a very special emphasis-that what is now presented to us with motion No. 14 is not clear enough. We are now discussing the over-all motion. Later on we will deal with each part and we will have an opportunity to move amendments and subamendments to clarify what needs to be clarified.
I think the government should take it upon itself to clarify the situation so that we may know exactly where we stand. For instance, what is meant by allocation of time? Will there be a minimum time? For a given debate, will the time allocated be one hour? Will provision be made in this motion so that, even if a specified time is allocated, each party shall at least have an opportunity to express its views?
No such provision is indicated in the motion, and I feel this is essential. The government should provide for something like that and add that the minister may move that a certain time be allocated for debate provided that each party in the house is given an opportunity to voice its opinion on each motion or that the minister may move that time be allocated provided such time is not less than one or two days. Nothing to that effect appears in the motion before us.
I suggest the government should take it upon itself to move the amendments and provide the clarification required on this matter.
In any case, when the time comes to move our own amendments, if the government has not done so, we shall feel duty-bound to do it in its place.

Members that the order restricts or cuts down. That is not true. It does restrict or cut down in some respects, but it is an attempt to restrict or cut down only with respect to those things which prevent the discussion of other matters which should be discussed. I hope that as the debate goes on it will come to be realized that this order is an attempt to get better programming of our work in Parliament.
It is, I think, interesting that both parts of this order set forth for the first time rights of an Opposition which heretofore have not been granted in a formal way. This point has

House of Commons Procedures not really been dealt with by any of the speakers who have preceded me. I hope, nevertheless, that it will be appreciated and I would welcome discussion of it, because I regard it as an important and significant feature.
I refer, for instance, to the first paragraph of the order in which the committee is asked to do certain detailed work in making the necessary changes in the rules dealing with supply. The committee is asked to consider this matter "including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed".

I have myself regarded the bringing for-word of estimates for discussion, within reasonable limits of protection to a Government, to be a right in the exercise of which the Opposition must play a prominent and very responsible part. I am not speaking now of the right of discussion of the matter in the House, but the right to have it brought forward for discussion. This is quite a new principle in the Canadian Parliament, and I think a very proper one, which is embodied here. It does afford protection to an Opposition against a Government using allocation of time in a way which might possibly preclude the Opposition from examining the items in question.
Similarly, in the proposal for allocation of time for legislation, the Opposition for the first time is brought in at the first stage to discuss allocation of time, to enter into the consideration of allocation of time. I regard this as a very proper method, because the activities of Parliament must be determined, in my view, not exclusively by the Government. It is quite true that the Government must take responsibility for legislation which it submits to Parliament; it must take exclusive responsibility for that and must stand or fall on it. Indeed, that is the basis of our whole system. But when it comes to Parliament's handling the legislation, I have always felt that the Opposition should have an active and full participation in the arrangements.
In our proposed changes in standing orders which deal with allocation of time for legislation, we have gone much further than has the United Kingdom Parliament. In the debate some interesting references have been made to the United Kingdom Parliament, but the Business Committee as they use the term there is something different from the Business Committee as we use the term in our proposal. Their Business Committee deals only with


the apportionment of time between different stages after the total time for it has been allocated, and in the United Kingdom, the Government takes the responsibility for the total allocation for the whole item. But we bring in the Opposition at the first stage under our proposed change to the rules, and I would think this is a significant feature in protecting the Opposition against some of the fears which have been expressed.
There have also been one or two unfortunate references in the press comparing this rule with the United Kingdom rule. While it is true that some parts of it are modelled on the United Kingdom rule, to make a comparison on a total, over-all basis is quite wrong and misleading; because the United Kingdom rule and practice in this respect goes far beyond anything which even the sharpest critic of this proposed rule suggests is harsh in the present proposal. Therefore I hope there will not be any generalizations made in comparing the two, because the United Kingdom rule relating to allocation of time is very much harsher than our suggested procedure.
For example, our procedure requires for the first time that a Minister rise and request that an allocation of time be considered by the Business Committee. The effect is to give all Members of the House of Commons notice, so they will know what is going on before the Business Committee. I must take some responsibility for putting in that provision, and I did so because I have sensed, through my limited experience as House Leader since my appointment was announced on November 1 last that Members of the House sometimes have not been aware that house leaders were dealing with certain subjects in an attempt to program the business of the House. I hope this requirement that a Minister must rise and make this request will give those private Members notice so they can immediately communicate as they wish-this is their own private affair-with their representative on the Committee. I think this is quite important because on a couple of occasions at least I have suspected, and I think with some reason, that hon. Members have not been aware of this. The time required for the procedure is also rather interesting.
The Minister having given notice on one day, the representatives on the Committee are given three days to try to reach agreement on some reasonable program for dealing with the proposed legislation. If they agree, then there is a procedure provided for making an

order of the House. Assuming they fail to agree, then, and only then, can a Government Minister announce that the next day he is going to give notice of a motion dealing with allocation of time. One day's notice is given. Therefore one day elapses before the motion comes up for discussion, and there is a full day's debate on the motion which is put forward in that way.
Another difficulty which has arisen in the meetings we have been having is this. When there seems to be a general consensus among the representatives after considering this matter, there is no provision for making it an order of the House except by unanimous consent of all Members. I think we have rather-I think I could use the word-"stumbled" into a situation where we have a Virtual veto by one Member which can frustrate the will of the vast majority of those on both sides of the House in all parties to have some programming which would permit other business to be brought before the House, or would permit a recess. We have found quite some difficulty on this point, and an attempt has been made under the proposed rules to provide a remedy.

In my view, it is necessary at this stage of our parliamentary history to develop a system of programming the business of the House. As I indicated in my remarks, while proving the necessity for this is probably fairly easy, how to achieve a solution is more difficult.

If I am correct in sensing that this feeling may also be in the minds of other hon. Members, as I think it may well be from what I have heard in private discussions, I want to make it quite clear now that we are ready to provide an assurance that the power will not be abused by setting drastic limits on debates. In that regard perhaps we can work out some formula or some minimum time for each of the stages which can be inserted in the paragraph. Incidentally, this point was also raised by the hon. Member for Lapointe. If we can mutually agree, we are prepared to insert a minimum time limit for all stages of a measure or for each stage of a measure separately, as the case may be, so that no motion can be made to set a time shorter than this minimum. In drafting the rule it had not been visualized that that difficulty could arise because what we were thinking of was trying to prevent the consensus of the House being frustrated by what could become virtually the veto of one Member. Therefore, before we meet on Tuesday I should like to consult with the House leaders about the precise terms for such an amendment. I should like to feel free to do that.
At the same time I should like to look at another point that has become apparent and was rather well dealt with by Members last night in the debate. I refer to the question relating to the supply part of the proposed order. Before I deal with that, perhaps I should deal with another point that has been raised privately by some hon. Members opposite and has been mentioned in the House by the hon. Member for Royal on another item of business.
The Prime Minister gave the assurance that we would include an amendment making It possible to extend the time allocation in any case where the Government introduced an amendment of a substantial character at a late stage in the consideration of a measure already being debated under an allocation of time. Obviously it would be unfair, after an allocation of time had been set, for the Government to bring forward an amendment of a substantial nature and use up the time

House of Commons Procedures allocated on some really new subject matter. I should like to meet with the house leaders to draft an amendment that will provide adequate protection on this point. It is dealt with specifically, of course, in the Prime Minister's speech.
I want to emphasize again, as the Prime Minister emphasized in his opening speech, that what we are seeking to do is not in any way to restrict legitimate debate or to reduce the time required for adequate consideration of a measure, but to make it possible to have arrangements for the orderly consideration of business and to ensure that after full debate, decisions can be reached. There may be one or two smaller points to be dealt with in the supply part of the order.
I should like to speak more fully about the precise method of dealing with what is set out in the subamendment and in the amendment. The point made in the subamendment about final supplementary estimates is a perfectly valid point of objection to the wording of paragraph 1 of the proposed resolution, and we propose to accept that in some form. But the other point about taking out all the supplementaries is not a valid point, because so many of the supplementaries are discussed when the main estimates are considered. It is not a satisfactory way of meeting the difficulty which the hon. Member foresees.
Then there is the question of taking out the supply motions. I do not think that is a satisfactory remedy. I think they ought to be included in the time limitation, but I believe there is room for amendment of the standing order dealing with the six supply motions because I realize that the rules on that point are not in a satisfactory state. I should like to hear the views of members of the Opposition in that regard.

speechtext: Yes, we hope that the acceptance of the proposal now before the House will make it possible to program the business of the session in such a way as to make provision for the handling of the major part of the business of the session in an adequate way, and also-and it is important we should be realistic-to permit business to be laid before the House in such a way that we can, with certainty, fix, for instance, the times for the Christmas recess, the Easter recess and the summer recess. It is my view quite firmly, as a result of my experience here over a number of years, that any realistic appraisal of a Member's duty to his constituents implies, if he is to perform his functions here efficiently, the proper contacts with his constituency and also, I might add, with his family and that provision must be made for the appropriate recesses.

speechtext: A second question. I think it is generally conceded by all Members that when we discuss estimates nowadays we are really discussing Government policy rather than the financial aspects of the estimates. Anyway, that has been the case since I came to the House. Some attention should be paid to this situation before we are asked to embark on the new system which is now proposed. Let us assume that a committee studies the estimates of a particular department. Under the British parliamentary system such a committee would report to the House on the estimates it has studied and certain days would be set aside for discussion and action on the report. Here in Canada the difficulty has always been this: A report is tabled but it is left to the Government to decide whether the points raised in it are taken up or not. The Leader of the House is well aware of this problem and I am wondering what arrangements are to be made for having the report of the committee discussed, or accepted or rejected by a majority of the House in a formal way so that the work of the committee would not be wasted, as so often happens now.

Before proceeding with the remarks I had intended to make I should like to refer for a few moments to the questions which have been asked by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) because they raise issues which I feel are important.
I think the question raised by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre as to the time during which committees should sit and the manner in which they should carry out their business is an important one. We have all experienced the problems which arise when a committee summoned for ten o'clock or ten thirty does not meet until eleven o'clock leaving it with an hour and a half in which to examine witnesses or documents. Then the Members return to the House at two thirty, with an understanding that they must go back after orders of the day are over in order to complete the day's business. This, in my opinion, is an incomprehensible way in which to carry out these duties and is a complete waste of time.
We have developed in the Public Accounts Committee over a number of years, during the time His Honour the Speaker was chairman and subsequently, what I think is a far more interesting arrangement. Time is permitted for a Member of the committee to initiate a line of examination, to develop it fully and to complete it so that he will have made his point and elicited the information in which he is interested before letting another Member of the committee have the floor. But within the limited period of an hour and a half or two hours, with the doubtful probability of being able to carry on at 
a later time, this whole scheme would fall by the wayside unless the House and the Government give attention to the machinery which is to be provided to implement the desires of the Government and of hon. Members in this regard. This relates to what the hon. Member for Timiskaming had to say about committee reports. A committee report may be filed, but if no motion for concurrence is moved it perishes. Not all committee reports need be the subject of discussion in the House, though there are many which ought to be.

This would impose certain limitations upon deliberations in Committee of Supply. My argument relates to committee reports as a whole, and I would think the Government might give consideration to a means whereby if committee reports were filed, and no motion is made to concur, they should be brought to the floor of the House for consideration and debate upon notice being given by a definite number of Members. Of course the Government does not need to accept such a report, but there would be an opportunity to debate it to a limited extent; it would see the light of day.
This brings me to the question which was raised last night concerning the proposed amendment to Standing Order 43 section (2)-
When the debate on any motion made under Standing Order 15(2) is adjourned or interrupted, the order for resumption of the same shall be transferred to and considered under government orders.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Fickersgill) intimated that it was not the intention of the Government in proposing this change that the Government should interfere with or prevent a motion to concur in a committee report being brought back to the floor of the House.

He said, as the note appears in the proposals for changes which were published in the pamphlet issued in connection with these amendments, that the amendment would be only as to the order in which the motion to concur would be heard in order that the House be not deprived of its opportunity to ask oral questions and for the other routine proceedings to be held.
Some doubt was expressed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) about how that could be achieved, and I should like to throw out this suggestion for consideration. I suggest that a new item in the routine business of the House be established, to be known as Motions to Concur in Committee Reports. As to precedence of this order, it could appear in such a way as not to interfere with the proper rights of Members of the House to question the Government, or with the other routine proceedings which should have precedence over this. I throw out that suggestion so that before the debate is concluded the Government might give some consideration to it.
The President of the Privy Council intimated that, after hearing the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), he had been unclear as to what had been his views with regard to the particular resolutions which are before the House. I want to say that the very clear and categorical suggestion which was made by the Leader of the Opposition as to the fact that changes of this kind must be predicated upon our movement toward a greater degree of permanency in the Speakership was a very solid and valid point. I am quite unclear after listening to the President of the Privy Council as to what are his views on this suggestion.
During the course of his remarks he did indicate, as I thought, some dissent from the particular proposal advanced by the Leader of the Opposition; but as to the essence of the proposition itself, we are still in the dark as to what the Government is proposing. I think this is tremendously important, Mr. Speaker, because we have from time to time during the course of this debate heard mention of our moving towards some measure of conformity with United Kingdom practice, not in all matters but in some of the matters which are the subject of these suggested changes. There is no doubt about it that by custom and by practice there is in the United Kingdom today this desirable degree of permanency in the Speakership, which I think is fundamental if we are to achieve lasting benefit from these or any other changes in our rules.
House of Commons Procedures
For example, on one issue alone, when we come to consider the allocation of time proposal we immediately run up against the very, very difficult problem of amendments. Today we do not know in advance what amendments will be moved. We do not know the seriousness of some of the amendments, what may be involved in them, and what length of time must necessarily be spent in adequately discussing them. For instance, in a bill of some considerable length which has a large number of clauses in it I would suggest to hon. Members that it is utterly impossible to establish in advance a reasonable period of time for the proper consideration of all phases and stages of the bill. In the United Kingdom the practice is-and I will come to this in more detail later in my remarks-that very rarely is this allocation of time principle applied until a bill has reached committee stage, or it has been referred back from a standing committee. The Speaker in the United Kingdom has the authority under their Standing Orders to select the amendments to be moved. This is the only way in which, in my humble opinion, we can achieve any measure of stability in trying to adopt an allocation of time principle.
This is a very crucial and difficult situation. Would Members be prepared, under these circumstances, to place in the hands of the Speaker an advance list of their amendments written out in detail so that he could have the opportunity to select the amendments, group together those of a similar nature, and then permit the Business Committee-which operates in a different way in the United Kingdom, of course-with this information before them, knowing the nature and the number of the amendments, to establish the length of time a given bill at this particular phase of its passage should take? This matter is basic to the whole issue.
In the United Kingdom this is the practice because of the permanency of the Speaker. The Business Committee in the United Kingdom consists of the Chairman's panel, plus Members selected for each bill. The Chairman's panel is, in turn, selected by Mr. Speaker. I could go on and give a number of other reasons why, if we do propose to proceed along this path, we will be in great difficulty unless we at least move toward a greater degree of permanency in the Speakership.
Several suggestions have been made as to how this might be achieved. I for one would like to see the Speaker come from the House.

I realize this involves problems which have been mentioned both by the Prime Minister, and again last night by the Leader of the Opposition. But these are not insuperable obstacles. I suggest that we should direct our attention to solving these problems, and before this debate is over I should like to hear a categorical reply from the Government as to its position in this matter. He would have had an opportunity to exercise his knowledge of the rules. Another interesting facet of this which occurred to me is that the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre, had he been Speaker, might yet have achieved a reward which sometimes goes to Speakers by being elevated to the other place.

speechtext:
There he might have gained admiration for and knowledge of this institution; and who knows-at some time in the future we might have seen him leading a strong and sturdy battle to abolish the House of Commons.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is a difficult issue. It is an issue which has produced a debate of a very high order, I think. We have heard enunciations of high principles, and declarations of lofty and noble motives, so much so that to the uninitiated listening to this debate there might have occurred the thought: Why should people in a deliberative assembly of this kind who express sentiments of this nature worry about rules and orders? Surely they should be capable of governing themselves without subjecting themselves to standing orders. However, you and I who have
[Mr. Baldwin.)
DEBATES	May 21, 1665
been in this House for some time know that that is not the case.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I think it was Sir Erskine May who described the House of Commons by saying that in a large tumultuous assembly of this nature a few irregularities were bound to occur from time to time. The situation in this House of Commons is not different from that. There is a difficulty in all democratic assemblies relating to the reconciliation of two points of view which are often contradictory and seldom compatible.
There is a great need for orderly government and a strong urge for human dignity, decency and natural justice. Orderly government is very desirable, but by itself it is not enough. Very often orderly governments exist in concentration camps. I recall reading recently that Mussolini said on one occasion that one of his ambitions was to have the trains run on time in Italy. That is a very laudable ambition, Mr. Speaker, but obviously it is not sufficient. In our approach to problems, and particularly in our approach to the way in which we are going to modify the rules and Standing Orders, we must not lose sight of that very fundamental and desirable achievement of permitting all Members in their approaches to problems to have regard for human rights and freedoms. The difficulty we must face relates to reconciling our rules with these two provisions. I think this can be done.
I am in agreement with a number of the proposals which have been made, with certain alterations. That has been my position as stated in this House previously, and as a Member of the Committee on Procedure. Many of the principles inherent in some of these proposals are ones which I have supported, but there is some doubt in my mind as to whether the actual wording of the proposed changes now before us will in fact serve to implement the most desirable features of the changes I should like to see made. We need these changes.
There is no doubt that in the minds of the people of this country there is a strong feeling that this House and this Parliament could very usefully employ alterations, changes and improvements to its rules. This feeling is not peculiar to Canada, but common throughout the free world. The United Kingdom House of Commons at Westminster has a Committee on Procedure and Reform, and a request of hon. Members in that place was acceded to and an interim report in respect of changes
May 21, 1965

to the question period was brought down. Some hon. Members took exception to that report and one made a speech stating that there was a great need for radical and material changes. Throughout the state legislatures in the United States a strong demand is being made by the citizens and by legislators themselves for reform and changes. We are not alone in this regard, and the people of Canada are not alone in requesting these changes.
I think these changes are needed as a result of the powers given to the state to make considerable and serious alterations to our way of life. The state has entered into fields of activity never before contemplated, involving the expenditure of billions of dollars. I am sure those who were here before us never dreamed that those powers would lie within the spending power of Parliament. We are now in a period of transition and we are suffering the growing pains that accompany this kind of a change. That is why we need and must have rule changes.
However, because of this widespread feeling in the country the Government has to some extent taken advantage of the situation. The proposals which have been put before us, while based primarily on changes suggested by the committee, have in every case where there has been an issue been drafted in favour of the Government's view. Perhaps that is a natural thing, but we must look at them very closely for that reason. In that Committee on Procedure we had a great deal of give and take on the part of backbenchers -not necessarily party backbenchers, but backbenchers per se-regarding the views of the Government and the views of the Opposition parties. I think it is fair to say that everybody was reasonable and ready to compromise, as they did, but those compromises are not apparent in the detailed changes which we are now examining.
I welcome, taking it at its face value, the Prime Minister's statement at the time he introduced the first motion. At page 1477 of Hansard the Prime Minister is recorded as having said:
X know some Members have made suggestions in the last day or two. The hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) who presided so effectively over one of the subcommittees has mentioned changes he would like to see and there will undoubtedly be others. I think these possible amendments could be considered by the House-and I hope they will be-on an entirely non-partisan basis.
I take that as an assurance on behalf of the Government that these changes are nego-
House of Commons Procedures tiable and that suggested alterations will be considered. That view was reinforced by what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) said last night. If that is the case and the Government is not embarking upon a take-it-or-leave-it attitude, but is prepared to accept reasonable and honest amendments from all parts of the House, provided they are workable, I think we will accomplish a great deal. If that is not the case, I think we may find ourselves in a measure of difficulty in this regard, because as much as I favour the principles involved, I would find great difficulty in persuading myself to accept in toto, without any qualifications, everything that is contained within the four corners of these two motions.
Before I continue very briefly to deal with the two specific proposals contained in the first motion, I should like to refer to a reference made to absenteeism by an hon. Member one or two days ago. I think there is a formidable difficulty in regard to absenteeism, particularly if it is related entirely to recorded votes. Recorded votes do not represent a criterion, as all too often it has been taken to be, of the measure of attendance of an hon. Member in this House, or as a measure of the effectiveness with which an hon. Member works.
There have been placed before this House by way of amendments certain proposals in respect of which, so far as I am concerned, there was no clearcut issue for one to make a decision and cast a vote. Not very long ago a subamendment was proposed to the budget motion by the hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). I do not intend to trespass the rule which states that we must not reflect on previous motions, but I wish to make a short reference to this subamendment to illustrate my point.
The subamendment involved a principle which appealed to me, and was related to a reduction in taxes. However, having regard to the value in dollars and cents and the degree to which the amount of money would be collected in some other form of taxation, I could not in the time available come to any decision. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pennell) did mention a figure in relation to the dollars and cents value. I do not know how he arrived at that figure, but it was not supported by statistical information. I suggest that if a Member had time to consider the subamendment and its results, and had access to certain information, he could come to a decision,
1578	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures but not in the time that was available between the time that subamendment was proposed and when it was voted upon.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
To stop this I think that at some time, not necessarily now, we will have to have some way of dealing with these confidence votes so that when we do come to a real issue there will be an opportunity, through the means of standing committees or otherwise, for all the facts to be put on record, with the result that there will be no necessity for any Member having to cast his vote without a clear conscience because all of the facts on the issue are not available to him.
To go directly to the question of item 14 on the order paper, which deals, of course, with the detailed examination of estimates, I think this is very desirable. In my view, only in this way, with the Minister and his officials appearing before a committee and being subjected to examination by those Members who have informed themselves and who are knowledgeable and able to make inquiries as to the matters in which they are interested, will we get a proper, competent and critical study of the billions of dollars spent which are raised through taxes for the people of this country. In my opinion our responsibility to those who elect us, and to all the people of Canada, is not discharged by the kind of examination we have given to estimates in the past. This measure does provide a way, if the machinery is set up in the manner it should be.
As to the number of days allocated to the business of supply, I do not know whether this is too material although I think the Government has been somewhat harsh in its limitation. 1 think that included within the amendments proposed by the two hon. Members who spoke last night there is an opportunity for a more equitable distribution and allocation of time. In one particular I think we should be adamant in taking the stand that supplementary estimates of a particularly large amount should not be brought down after the 36 days allotted to the business of supply have been used up, and the House be asked to pass such estimates without any examination at all.

Yes, I did. I just wanted to reinforce the reasons why it should be done. As I understand the situation, the limiting of time is based on the fact that the estimates will be submitted to the standing committees. If it should happen that this does not take place, that safeguard will be lost. I have in mind the practice that has been followed all too frequently in my opinion of putting items in the estimates which are in fact legislation. I think of examples such as the bridge subsidy, certain subsidies and grants in the Department of Agriculture, the making of acreage payments and so on. If we are not protected by the adoption of an alteration of this kind, then I do not think we will be discharging our duty, and I was very happy to hear the President of the Privy Council say that this would in fact be done.
With regard to the question of allocation of time, I think we have to take a very hard look at this matter. As to the first part of the proposal I am in complete agreement. It follows in fact a proposal which emanated from the Committee on Procedure. With regard to the establishment of a Business Committee and the reference to that committee, on request of the Government, of any particular measure in order that the committee may take a look at it and try to work out in advance the period of days to be allotted to its consideration, if there is unanimity which would reflect the unanimity of all parties in the House their recommendation would, of course, be made an order of the House and there could not be any interference at a later date.
But I regard with some considerable suspicion and doubt the effect of subparagraph 5 of the proposed standing order 15A. As I indicated before, the practice in the United Kingdom has almost invariably been that only when a bill gets into the committee stage is an order made. The provision for making such an order is not contained in the Standing Orders. It is simply an inherent right of the House, not the Government, to make an order that a limited number of days be fixed as the time within which a particular measure shall be dealt with. Only after that is done is the matter referred to the Business Committee, which then considers in detail all of the proposed amendments and all of the aspects of the bill which would be involved in Committee of the Whole, and then third reading. Within the limited time that has been fixed by the House the Business Com-
May 21, 1965	COMMONS
mittee then allots the time that it considers necessary.
This would not be the case here. I can think of very dangerous situations involving a controversial measure with new and radical departures in our economic life which the Government might consider to be highly desirable but about which the Opposition might have grave doubts; and for the Government to attempt in advance to ask for and receive from the House a limited number of days for the discussion of every phase of such a bill would be catastrophic.
As a matter of fact, I think what might develop here will be a very reasonable type of practice. If the Government asks the Business Committee to set a limit on the number of days, it is in fact flashing an amber light. This is their D.E.W. line, their early warning system. The Government is saying: We think this measure is important but we think it is a measure with regard to which there should be a limited period of time for debate. If the representatives on the Business Committee come to the conclusion that the suggested length of time to be allocated is insufficient, there will no doubt be bargaining and negotiating as there is today. If there is irreconcilable conflict there will not be unanimity. The Opposition will have then indicated its position. With regard to a measure of this kind they may very well have strong, substantial and serious objections, and they will feel it is their right to ventilate and to put forward each and every one of these objections in at least a reasonably limited way.
This leaves the matter to the Government.
I can only see this procedure being applied in very rare cases on second reading; but when the bill reaches Committee of the Whole, as it will, the Government must then come to a decision whether it should grasp the nettle and limit the time. They have indicated their views and the Opposition Members have indicated their objections. If the Government then moves to fix an allotted time it then becomes an issue which eventually the people must decide. This is the kind of practice which I think will develop. I hope it will not be used too frequently. In the United Kingdom this particular provision has been used less than a dozen times in the last 10 years in respect of bills.
To what extent the Business Committee will supplant the present meetings between the House leaders is another question. It may well be that this committee will simply
DEBATES	1579
House of Commons Procedures be a meeting of the House leaders in another form. I do not know. But I do think there is merit in a Business Committee in this sense, that when there is unanimity at a certain stage it will be possible for the House to make a final order. However, I do urge the President of the Privy Council and the Members of the Government to be very careful about a procedure by which they fix well in advance the number of days to be allotted to all stages of a certain measure.
What about the situation where a measure may go to the Senate and come back with amendments? Will this be included? I just mention this as one possibility which the Government may not have considered. There are many dangerous traps in this procedure if it follows the path that is outlined.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
As to the principle, yes; I feel as I said before that there should be greater opportunity for the Government, as the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said, to do things. However, I should like more opportunity to stop the Government from doing things, if I think they are doing things which are not right, as would other hon. Members. I should like more opportunity to seek to mould the minds and change the policies of the Government, either as represented in the estimates or in respect of bills. I should like this opportunity, an opportunity which under the present system is not given as effectively as it well might be. So, in that sense, I agree with the principle, but as to the details I have grave doubts.
There is one more point I should like to mention. I make this further suggestion to the Government, that they might consider continuing, not at this session but possibly next session if they are here to do so, the Committee on Procedure and Reform of the Rules. I have a number of reasons for making this suggestion. There is no doubt in my mind that if these rules are adopted certain consequences will flow from them which are not contemplated at this time. I have the feeling that these proposals have been rather hastily put together following the end of the last session. I am quite convinced that certain things will come about which we do not contemplate at this time. I believe as well that if the particular proposal by which appeals from Mr. Speaker's ruling are abolished, it might not be a bad idea to have in existence a committee which would be seized of an understanding of these rules, and which would meet from time to time and to which
1580	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures Mr. Speaker could have access. This would not at all in any way deny the right to have the fullest and complete discussions in the House. Certainly, if the right of appeal is abolished I would hope-I am quite convinced that this would happen-that there would be offered a most adequate opportunity for discussion in this House of any phase of the matter under debate. But I believe a panel of this kind would serve a very useful function.
Then we find from time to time that the rules must be changed. Our experience has been that the period of gestation from the time when the change has been desirable until it has gone through the process of being considered in this committee, brought back for consideration by the parties, going back to the committee again and ultimately coming to the House, is anywhere from one to three years. For this reason, I think the suggestion might be useful.
I have one other suggestion to make before I resume my seat. This deals with what I believe is a lamentable omission on the part of the Government, their failure to include a committee on delegated powers. I heard the explanation given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that they are contemplating the appointment of a royal commission to deal with the question of the appointment of an ombudsman. In my opinion, the extent to which governments in the past few years have been moving more and more toward a delegation of authority from the legislative to the executive branch requires the establishment of a committee of this kind. In Northern Ireland, as I understand the procedure, all Orders in Council which are passed which delegate certain authority to the executive must be laid before the House of Commons within a limited time. If they are not so laid before the House, they cease to be effective. This is rather drastic. I do not believe we could do this. It is my submission, having in mind the experience over the past few years and the present, for example the fact that the current Budget resolutions contain very drastic delegations of authority from the legislative to the executive branch, that one of the great needs we have in any legislative body in this day and age is the right to review the extent to which a Government has exercised this power to delegate authority and to be criticial of it when we find the need arises.

Mr. Speaker, during last session I had the privilege and honour to sit on the committee on procedure and organization with some hon. members who have a very great experience in the field of parliamentary procedure which is so difficult and complicated. I must tell you at once that owing to the fact that I sat with highly experienced members including the hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and some others, I have acquired a certain experience myself which I hope will be very useful to me in the future and will enable me to discuss with more assurance and more ability the business of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I was really disappointed, after the committee had met so often last year-there were more than thirty general sittings, in addition to the many sittings of the subcommittee on procedure-to find out, at the end of last session, that it was not decided to accept the changes suggested in the procedure of the house.
However, I note with pleasure that the government itself has now decided to propose to the house the procedural changes and, after listening to the remarks of the few hon. members who spoke before me, I am sure that there will be unanimous approval to the proposal brought before the house by the government.
During the next few minutes I shall endeavour to express my views on some of the proposed changes. Of course, I have mixed feelings about them, because I would have liked the government to go a bit further. But Paris, Ottawa or Canada were not built in a day and I think this is a first step toward an improved procedure for the business of the house.
I am glad to find that one of the main suggestions made by the committee during last session has been accepted and that, from now on, the detailed examination of the estimates will be limited to 36 days.
Like many of my colleagues, I have listened to the arguments put forth by previous speakers and there is no doubt that what we have here is quite an improvement.
I think that 36 days should be long enough to discuss the estimates. It means practically seven weeks of continuous debate and I think it is amply sufficient for such consideration.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has suggested an amendment to extend that period by ten or 12 days for a total of nine or ten weeks. We all know, Mr. Speaker, the wide experience of the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre in this field. I wonder if, at a time when decisions have to be taken quickly, when the business of government is in the process of re-organization to cope more efficiently with the many and complex problems facing it each day, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would not change his attitude as far as the number of days required for the discussion of estimates. Whether we like it or not, there are only 365 days in a year; therefore, we have to manage with that number of days to cope with the existing situation, in an era of automation where electronic machines are used to expedite work as much as possible. The House of Commons would operate more slowly by extending debate on these problems. It is not a question of days, Mr. Speaker, it is a question of expediting seriously the business before the house. Surely, the members are capable of self-discipline so that detailed examination of estimates may be done within a reasonable period of time, but not too long a period to delay consideration of other urgent problems.
I also know that this motion calls for the allocation of a time limit for the examination of any question or any stage of a question introduced before the house.
For a long time now the members have been aware that the House, as far as possible, should be informed about the period allowed for a bill or for the stage of a bill in order that it can plan its business and thus expedite it.
Mr. Speaker, the time is past when anyone could freely decide how long a bill or one of its stages would be discussed.
As I said a few minutes ago, we are living in an age where everything is mechanized, and it is quite difficult to find the time required to do everything we have to do. We should know in advance how much time we will have to study a bill.
The time is past also where a political party, an organization, a member of a group could take advantage of those new rules to trample under foot the rights of Parliament.
The news media are adequately organized today; radio and television inform the people adequately and quickly about current events; and this information is readily available to all information media, so that under our

That leads me to believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is absolutely essential to allocate a period of time for the consideration of any bill at any stage, in order to expedite in a practical and useful way the work submitted to us.
As to the extension of sitting hours, I would be a little less sanguine about it. To me this is a moot question. Indeed, what matters is whether the house should have more time to consider the issues placed before it.
If the hours of work were increased it would no doubt be logical to expect a greater amount of work. However, there is a limit to human activity and, besides, there are other problems for the members of the house to cope with. I am not opposed to that suggestion because, in my opinion, the parliament-it is not only the government-should have the right to extend its own sitting hours. But I think this is a right which should be exercised with moderation.

I think above all that the house should be informed at least one day in advance or at least at the beginning of every sitting, because today there is not only the agenda problem, but also that of the staff members who must know in advance how much time will be available either to rest or to plan their work. There is no doubt that by extending the hours of sitting, some staff members will be overworked.
I believe that the mere extension of the hours of sitting will not ensure the appointment of an additional chief in the English debates or of an additional chief of the French debates section. I am convinced that the number of positions will not be doubled but, on the other hand, the work load of some staff members of the house will certainly increase. That is why I feel the government or parliament should proceed with caution when examining the possibility of extending the hours of sitting.
I understand that the extension of the hours of sitting would especially benefit private members' business. Once more, I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that attendance in the house would not be worthy of the speeches delivered. I wonder if it would be possible not to record or take down in shorthand the speeches which would then be delivered. In the House of Commons in England, I think that arrangements have been made some

time ago to reduce the number of speeches taken down in shorthand after certain hours.
One of the proposals which I would heartily endorse is the suggestion that appeals from the Speaker's rulings should be abolished. Abuse of the right to appeal from such rulings undoubtedly undermines the authority and especially the importance of that office. Some have suggested that the time may be ripe to appoint a permanent Speaker. I am in complete agreement with that proposal, and I feel that parliament should seriously consider that question in the very near future. Everyone seems to be agreed on the advisability of implementing that suggestion but opinions are still divided, or at least, there does not seem to be unanimity concerning the way to appoint the Speaker. Should he be elected by the people or appointed by the house? Should he represent a particular riding? Those are points which have not yet been cleared up. The question surely deserves serious consideration and a solution should be found soon so that the house may be presided over by a person worthy of that office and especially one who has the confidence of all hon. members.
As for questions of privilege, which have increased steadily in the past few years and which sometimes are asked without a valid reason, I think that by requiring that they should be tabled in writing at least one hour before they are asked, many of them will be eliminated, because this will provide for a sort of cooling off period during which the eagerness and the sudden reactions that the members of the house may quite normally feel after a word, a sentence or a decision they might consider for a moment as a breach of some privileges, will wear off.
Moreover, the fact that the calling of the orders of the day is restricted to 30 minutes will leave much more time to the house for the consideration of the legislation before it and, therefore, I believe that the need to extend the sitting hours will not be so great; besides, this will enable the ministers who have to manage the business of the country to give more time to their work in the best interests of our citizens.
In regard to the period when the orders of the day are called, may I suggest that 2:30 p.m. does not seem to be the best time. My short experience as a member of the house has taught me that at the most important time of the day, that is at 2:30 p.m., the ministers of the crown are required to be in the house in the event a question is put to them. Since the questions put on the order

paper and the other business have to be dealt with, that question period, even if it lasts only for 30 minutes, can sometimes extend until four o'clock and even 4:30 on Wednesdays.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Consequently, at the time of the day when it would be important that a minister be in his office, devoting his time to the business of his department, he has to sit in the house in the event of a question being asked or a problem being drawn to his attention.
I heard many comments on that from persons who tried to meet ministers at a definite time but who found it impossible, for the good reason that the ministers had first to be in the house and did not know till what time they would have to stay.
I also noted that certain people had unfortunately to wait for hours, and I am now speaking of persons who had been invited by the ministers themselves for the purpose of discussing a piece of legislation or very important problems.
These persons had to cool their heels in the ministers' waiting room from 2.30 in the afternoon till 7 or 8 in the evening before being able to discuss the problem they wanted to submit to them or for which they had been invited to come to their offices.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, Canada is an important nation engaged in too urgent and too serious matters, which require prompt consideration and decision, to afford this waste of time, indeed this waste of energy, not only of the ministers but of those who come to consult them. In fact, I know that even certain deputy ministers have to wait before seeing the minister; they must stay in the house in the event of a question being asked of the head of their department. Our nation is too important to afford such a waste of energy.
Mr. Speaker, I propose that the house examine seriously the suggestion I often made, and which was made to me by several persons, to the effect that the question period be postponed until eight or nine o'clock at night, or even 9.30, but preferably eight o'clock, which would be the right time, since written questions could be submitted to the Speaker until six o'clock p.m. At that time the Speaker could determine what questions are relevant and which are out of order, together with those which should appear on the order paper. Then, around 6.30 or seven o'clock, the Speaker could send the various ministers or officials of the departments a copy of the questions which should be answered and which would be called automatically at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of good procedure, of planning the business of the house. We must know exactly where we are going, we must organize the business of the house so that it be more efficient, and consequently more interesting.
It is very interesting, of course, to sit here and listen to members' speeches, but sometimes one would like to know how long they will last, particularly if one has something else to do in which he might be more interested.
Mr. Speaker, another provision in this motion which is of particular interest to me is the one dealing with the establishment of standing committees of the house. I see their number is much greater, but their membership has been reduced, except for the committee on agriculture, forestry, and rural development.

I fully support this suggestion that committees should be composed of 22 members, instead of 36, 40 or 45. In fact, it is easier to work with 22 members, to perform a task in a more intelligent manner and in less time than it would require with 45,	40 or even 36
members.
Of course, considering the fact that 21 committees are to be instituted, composed of 22 members only, there will be less overlapping of committees.
Indeed, until now, one could be a member of a 45 member committee and at the same time of another committee of 36 members. Under the proposed system, the work will be more expeditious and more effective.
Mr. Speaker, I also notice that an excellent suggestion is being made, which had been made by the committee on procedure and organization, namely that any member of parliament, even though he would not be a member of a standing committee, could have the right to speak in a committee. I realize that it is only normal for him not to have the right to vote and not to be included in the number of members required for a quorum, but to allow a member of parliament to share in the proceedings of a
House of Commons Procedures committee, although he may not be a member of the said committee, is certainly an improvement. Members cannot sit on every committee they are interested in, but, at any given moment while a certain committee is sitting, a problem of interest to a particular member might come up. This member will then be able to take part in the discussion, in other words, to satisfy his curiosity or contribute to the good work of that committee by submitting his views.
Mr. Speaker, all this leads me to suggest that the resolution now before us is of the utmost importance and I hope it will be approved unanimously, so that, thanks to these new rules, the house may be able to proceed with its work more rapidly and efficiently.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, I know there will be some who, because of their fine sense of tradition, will be opposed to these rules which they might find too drastic or revolutionary.
Mr. Speaker, I read in today's issue of Le Devoir an editorial by Mr. Claude Ryan. It is true that this article does not apply to the problem of procedure under consideration today, because he dealt with it at length and with tact a few days ago. I should like, however, to quote a sentence which, in my opinion, is especially relevant to the problem now before us. Mr. Ryan states:
-in an organization as complex and ramified as the government of a modern state, it would not he realistic to attempt to introduce, at the top of the government, a narrow and literal collegialism which would seek to reduce the role of the head of a government to that of the chairman of a board of directors.
Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, the time has come to decide not only to look into the problems requiring our immediate attention, but to provide also for the future. I think I am right in saying that we often consider bills that should have been passed one, two or even three years ago and that a number of bills are waiting on the shelves in various departments because we simply did not have the time to introduce and consider them.

I am-like other members of this house, -not only surprised but also sorry to put it mildly about this situation when one considers that we are studying bills which could have been passed two, three, four or five years ago, and that we are hardly providing for the future.
If we do not want this generation or the one coming up to treat us as the old guard-

Let us give a little freedom to the gov-erment if we want to keep pace with progress, mechanical and scientific, in this pushbutton and missile era.

Mr. Speaker, after sitting in this house for three years, during which I looked around, studied and listened as much as I could, because it is better for one to wait until he has some experience before he launches into public affairs-there are examples I am glad to consider and follow-there is a thought I should like to leave with the hon. members, and it is this. If we do not keep pace with the times, the next generation will deny us, no matter what side of the house we belong to. On the other hand, if this house sets an example of business quickly and well done, with modern rules which do not fence the government in a narrow and vulnerable collegialism, but grant it a certain leeway, we may not have to face, when we least expect it, situations which we may believe to be revolutionary at first sight but which,

in my opinion, would merely result from our inefficiency.

I am glad we are considering this motion because a number of very important changes are included. Several things have been said so far in this debate in relation to important matters, and one had reference to the attendance in this House. In my opinion the attendance here has been grim. Perhaps that is a direct result of the fact that many Members elected to serve here expected to find something different and have been disillusioned. If that is the case, I can assure those Members that they are not alone in that unhappy position. I believe the general population of this country finds itself in exactly the same position.
The Prime Minister has seen fit to move these proposed changes in our procedure and I think he ought to be here to defend, not what is included in these proposed changes, but what has not been included. I have read in part May's Seventeenth Edition and the Standing Orders of the British Parliament, from which our Standing Orders have been taken. It is interesting to note that we
