an excellent job in examining the estimates of the departments referred to them. Is it not a fact, though, that nothing really happened in connection with the deliberations of the committee? In the United Kingdom they have found that they had to refer the report of the committee to the Government as a basis for discussion of the estimates. If we discuss the estimates of the Department of National Defence in a select committee on estimates, then we do not need to discuss them again in the House.
I believe that Members of Parliament are wasting their time in most of the committees with which I have had any experience. If you do not believe that, Mr. Speaker, you should attend some of these committees and wait around for an hour or two. You will find that very often there is not a quorum until a considerable length of time has passed. A very few minutes after the committee gets started the quorum again disappears and the Chairman usually asks if he can ignore the fact there is no quorum because the committee has important visitors there.
I believe that the Canadian people, in their wisdom, have elected the men they believe best suited to represent them. If these people go to a committee and walk out of it, or fail to turn up for the committee in the first place, then they do not see any advantage in the operations of the committee. In my opinion, they are not lazy. Hon. Members are not out of this House this afternoon because they want to go and play golf. They have decided it is much more advantageous to return to their ridings, talk to some of the people in that area and conduct some business in that area which they feel is more advantageous to them and to their people than sitting in this House. I believe this is true, and I think it is true of committees.
I shall cite an example. I believe it was foolish to sit for some time on the defence committee, then make a number of recommendations for simple changes which were ignored. I do not believe that the information we were provided by the various departments in conducting that inquiry would enable me or any of the other Members of the committee to say whether or not Canada should or should not engage in germ warfare development. I do not believe the information would enable us to decide whether the Arrow was a better weapon than the Bomarc. I do not believe we really had that kind of assistance in the committee. However, I do believe we arrived at a couple of conclusions. One of them was that we should standardize 22620-102
House of Commons Procedures nuts and bolts. We should not have store rooms full of 15 or 20 different sizes of nuts and bolts with different threads. These could have been replaced by standardized nuts and bolts with exactly the same threads so that they would be interchangeable without much difficulty with our allies who are producing the same type of equipment.
What happened to that report which was made to the House? I thought it was a sensible one. I do not believe anyone here, if asked individually, would disagree with the fact that it was a sensible report. Did the Minister discuss this? Did it ever come before the House so that the majority could make a decision? I doubt it. If it did, I do not remember it. Certainly, on several occasions I have heard the same matter discussed.
Let us take another example. We sat for some time on the Agriculture Committee when it considered the price of farm machinery. The present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) says that farm machinery costs are the greatest problem facing the farmer today.
I do not disagree with him. I do not believe there is anyone here representing a rural riding who would disagree with that statement. We did considerable research on this subject two or three years ago, the committee tabled its report and that report died right there. I do not know if the Government was in favour of it or opposed to it. I do not believe the Government gave a damn what happened to that particular report. We do not have the machinery to make the Government give some consideration to it. I do not really care if the Government turns it down or accepts it, but I feel I am wasting my time in this House if the majority does not sometimes make a decision.
There has been some suggestion today that one or two Members in this House have sometimes withheld unanimous consent to continue sitting. I am one of those Members. I make no apology for having withheld this consent on a number of occasions. Perhaps I am wrong, but I have found that when this House decides to close, then it closes. I do not believe a team of wild horses could get it closed until it is ready to close. I feel we should conduct business in an orderly fashion. I believe we should at least respect some of the niceties, and one of them is to treat the staff of this institution on at least a reasonable basis in terms of the hours they were hired to fill, and not continually extend the sitting into the small hours of the morning, missing lunch hours and so on or doing some of the other things that have been suggested.

I believe that the Government has to give some consideration to this matter of committees. It is not good enough to establish them and have them going in all directions, like a shotgun. They have to be funnelled back into the House. The House has to make some decision on these reports.

We disagree violently with the House leader if he is of the opinion that the debates conducted by a committee on specific estimates should be repeated in the House. If this were true, why do we then have the proposal to allow any Member interested in the subject discussed by a committee appear before that committee to make his point, even though he is not a member of the committee? Why do we have that proposal if we do not really intend, sooner or later, to have the committee complete its discussion and make a report which can be the basis of a debate, rather than have the individual item discussed again in the House? This, in my opinion, is the fundamental change that we are making. I believe that change has to be made. I believe that in this country we are not capable, as they found in the United Kingdom they were not capable, of doing what this gentleman Mr. Joseph Hume did in the early 1800's, of going over each item in the estimates and deciding whether or not the economies we expected had been made. We are not capable of doing that We do not have the research assistance to do it.
It has been said we can find someone who is stealing $5,000 from the estimates, but if someone were stealing $5 million it would be impossible for us to discover it. Occasionally we find horses on the payroll, but there are $15,000 or $20,000 people on it, and we will never catch up with them because we do not have the machinery. Let us not kid ourselves and tell the public we are examining the estimates. We are not. We are examining the policy of the Government in relation to the estimates. We are looking at the administration and the policy. We must face this, and to cope with the problem we must be provided with much better machinery.
The Prime Minister is not an expert on the rules and procedures of the House. He is not enamoured of the tradition of parliament, and this is a good thing. We have four or five Members who are very familiar with the technicalities of procedure, and I am surprised they have not been more strongly concerned during this debate with some of the changes that have taken place.

Holus-bolus we are stealing from the Standing Orders of the British House, but without keeping the protection provided by those orders. I could give instances of this by reading material on certain of these protections, from May's Seventeenth Edition. Our four or five experts should give attention to that matter.

Not at the moment. As I have said, the mover of these proposals is not an expert in the field of procedure, but I sincerely believe what he said about the necessity for making a change. I am sure he is proposing these changes in the hope that they will do what is expected of them. I may be a cynic, but I have never yet seen a rule that one could not get around. I might have made a good lawyer if I had the intelligence and perhaps the opportunity to study law, because I believe no rule has ever been made that one cannot get around, and if I do not particularly like these new rules I may try to prove that some day.
We are all sincerely interested in having things done within a certain period of time. We all have an obligation and a responsibility but we should not be subjected to the electioneering that takes place in the House almost all the time. These proposals are designed this way, and almost everything that comes before Parliament is designed this way.
I remember the list of strategic items which the Government said it had to place before Parliament last session, but we did not spend our time dealing with them. We spent our time on two items that were not included in that list. We went off on a political tangent into another field. The country does not deserve that. The public will not put up with it too long, and it behooves all of us to look closely at the rules and see what compromises can be made.
The Government must agree that the Opposition has the right to look into administration and policy in financial matters, and this can only be done by examining the estimates. It may be done in 26 days; it may be done in less. But if this time limit is set it is like setting a floor price, and at the end of it we will be faced with much more work to do.
Since I have been a Member of the House, I have seen such things as supplementary estimates go through without discussion. In-

terim supply has gone through without any discussion; but this happened at a time when discussion had already been allowed on a wide range of related subjects. We had a complete picture of the financial problems, and so this did not warrant a rehashing of the matters because of changing circumstances and new issues.
The Government must consider a timetable. The Parliament of Great Britain has given great consideration and study to this matter. It has made mistakes which it has had to correct. Surely we can take full advantage of the protections it has written into its rules, and not make similar mistakes ourselves.
If the orders are altered with respect to discussion of estimates, then the committees to which estimates are referred should give full consideration to them. The Minister responsible should be on call at all times, if the committee desires to have him present. His officials, and the officers appointed to the committee should provide it with all the assistance necessary to go into the details of the financial aspect of the estimates. In addition, the Government should refer the administration of policy to the committee for its consideration. If all this is done, then there is no reason why the estimates, when they come back to the House, should be discussed other than on the basis of the committee's report.
It is foolish to tell the country, and it is foolish for the newspapermen to be so blind as to think that just because a discussion is going to take place in the committee, this will solve any particular problem. If the committee does its job it will submit a reasonable report to the House, but if its report is tabled, never to be discussed again or given consideration by the Government and the House, then the committee will not have served any purpose except to educate Members in the limited field to which it has turned its attention, so that they will be experts in that field when discussing it in Committee of the Whole House on supply.
I believe the Government will have to decide to set three or four months aside for consideration of the financial aspects of the nation. During that period the Budget should be produced, and the committees set up immediately under a Standing Order specifying a certain date. The parties could be given three or four days to nominate their committee Members, and the Government allowed one or two days to establish the committees and the chairmen, and refer the estimates to them.

When that period is ended there should be no further review of the financial situation except for those things included in supplementary estimates. In my opinion, this should also include interim supply, because it seems very odd to pass interim supply when the Government is asking for twelve twelfths of the estimates. Interim supply was never expected to provide that.
Something else the Government has not considered is that when it lifted Standing Orders from the British House it did not consider the fact of the difference between the British North America Act and the custom in the British House. In the U.K., under standing order 43, they establish a Business Committee which has the power to make recommendations, but in Canada we are to some extent bound by the B.N.A. Act which states that in this country decisions shall be made in the House by a majority of the Members voting in the House. I am not a lawyer and I do not know how the Government will resolve the contradiction between the British North America Act and Standing Orders. The situation here is not the same as the situation in Great Britain and this fact has not been given full consideration.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
A number of other matters might be discussed. One is the suggestion that a permanent Speaker be appointed. I am not going to say the nice things that some other Members have said about Speakers. It is good to say all these things. I am not referring to the present incumbent of the Chair, but let us take a look at what happens in the operation of this House. I think anyone looking at the position would be shocked to find some of the things that are happening. A number of senior officials who now, one could say, run the House of Commons, will shortly have to be replaced. No provision has been made for successors to take over. Political considerations will arise which really detract from the rule of the Speaker in our parliamentary system. We have an Internal Economy Commission consisting only of Members of the treasury branch, four or five senior Cabinet Ministers who make the decisions. This is a completely unsatisfactory way of running our affairs. I would be happy to go into this at greater length because this is a subject which would have to be considered, and the time to do so is now, before we decide that a permanent Speaker should be appointed. At that time, of course, we would have to decide the manner in which
1590	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures he would be appointed-whether he would have a seat in the House of Commons within the precincts of Parliament Hill or not. In any case the Internal Economy Commission will need to be constituted differently so that Members of Parliament chosen by the people will be able to run the operation of the House as is the case in the United Kingdom.
Senior officials of this House should long ago have been sent to the United Kingdom or Australia or some of the other Commonwealth countries where they have parliamentary governments in order to acquire the necessary training. Part of the abuse in this House is that the advice given to the Speaker is usually political advice rather than impartial advice. You may wonder why Members do not turn all their questions in to the Speaker. Well, I can remember former Speakers receiving these questions. Shortly afterward Members of the Government were able to stand up and give an answer they should not have known at all. These implications should not be there. I may be wrong in drawing an inference. There may have been some namby-pamby in the operation of this. I am not saying the Speaker was involved. But these things will have to be considered before we appoint a permanent Speaker.
I agree a committee should be set up. I do not think the previous committee failed in its duty. It arrived at some excellent conclusions, a number of which I would be more interested in supporting than I am in the proposals now before us. But that committee only scratched the surface of the problem which faces Parliament. It was brash of the Government to introduce these proposals for change when there was so much prospect of getting general agreement in the previous committee. The theme to be borne in mind when changing the rules is that general agreement should be sought because the more such changes are brought about by general agreement the better democracy will work. When someone feels that autocratic rules are being used against him specifically,
I believe they will not last very long or produce the results people thought they would.
In conclusion, I am convinced the Canadian people are very much in favour of a change in our rules. I believe this view is endorsed by practically every Member of the House. Many of the backbenchers are completely dissatisfied with the operation of Parliament. They feel frustrated here and deprived of any opportunity to use their ability. An improve-

DEBATES	May 21, 1965
ment could be brought about as a result of some of the proposals before us today. The changes suggested are worth while, but will not be effective unless we ensure that the work a Member does in committee can be translated into policy, either accepted or turned down by the Government. Members who have worked very hard in committee are frustrated to find that their efforts have led to no conclusion. Unless the Government reaches decisions on all these proposals I do not think the new system will work satisfactorily.
To be fair, there are some Cabinet Ministers who look with interest on what is done in the committees. There are Ministers who have gone out of their way to take up suggestions made in these committees and implement them. I realize, too, that the Government has to face its own responsibility of deciding whether or not the time to implement a decision taken by a committee has arrived. A government has to exercise that responsibility and it is capable of doing so. But the Cabinet has got so far away from the ordinary Members of this House that backbenchers on the other side are less aware of what their leaders are doing than we who sit in this corner of the House.
During the time I have served as a Member I have been able to gain some knowledge of the workings of most of the departments, through the senior executive officers. As the requests which reach a Member multiply, his insight into the operations of the various departments increases and his scope broadens. This experience enables him to by-pass what might well appear to be an insurmountable block. But for most Members there is great frustration in parliament. The Government of the day, the previous Government and, indeed, every administration, faces or has faced the fact that a number of its supporters do not intend to run for re-election because they feel they are doing nothing by continuing to serve in the House of Commons, despite the fact that many are competent people who have, by the nature of things, been unable to play a proper role in the system.

Member called it, this very exclusive establishment, and I got the impression that deep down, as members of this club in which they won their laurels and gained experience of the rules, they may not be as keen to see reforms of our rules and procedure.
The Leader of the Opposition gave a brief but very eloquent history of parliament, but I am wondering whether the right hon. gentleman was not standing a little too close to the canvas instead of going back far enough to see whether the framework of our parliamentary system really suits Canada or Canadians. I think the right hon. gentleman will acknowledge that from its beginning Parliament has always been a reviewing and reexamining body; it has never been an initiating body. I think the Leader of the Opposition will acknowledge as an historian that from its inception the Government has been appointed by the Crown, whether under
DEBATES	1591

Parliament was called upon in order to pass new levies of taxation, at which time the serfs, the knights and the commoners came to this assembly, to the House of Commons or parliament, and expressed their grievances, being listened to by the government. They then went home.
The brutal truth is that, really, parliament has not changed in essence since that time. All of us are here merely to review, to criticize and to express grievances. Very few of us, in fact no hon. Member, actually takes the initiating step in the matter of legislation.
At one time it was said that government proposes, parliament disposes. I think it can now be said that the establishment-the Prime Minister said it is expert officialdom-proposes, government disposes and parliament merely opposes; and I think that is the truth.
This brings forward the real issue underlying these resolutions, which is this: Do Canada or Canadians want, or will they accept, a very expensive body which reviews and re-examines, or do Canada and Canadians want Members to take the initiating step in the matter of legislation? My experience is brief, but I receive letters from constituents, as do all backbenchers, to this effect: "Dear Member, make sure that so and so is done; make sure that the exemptions are increased; make sure pensions are increased". Little do these poor misguided constituents know there is very little communication, in fact no communication at all, between backbenchers and other Members and the Government.

The hon. Member for Carleton suggests that, having 11 bills, it is understandable that I was confused, but I was confused that day by other things than the 11 Bills.
This bill came to my mind, Mr. Speaker, after reading this book, which is noted in the bibliography "The Grim Truth About Mutual Funds", by Ralph Lee Smith, published by Putnam in 1963. Mr. Smith is a former head of the National Better Business Bureau in the United States.
The book hit me with a considerable impact because I think that, like every other part of the country, my community has been swimming in salesmen for mutual funds and
May 21, 1965

Criminal Code
mutual trust companies. Every time we turn around it seems that there is someone selling for these companies, and it may be an air force corporal or a garage station attendant. I am not saying anything about people in these walks of life being mutual fund salesmen, but the plain fact of the matter is that, almost like the phenomenal growth rate which takes place in respect of various things every once in a while, there is a great rash of sales people now in the mutual funds field.
There has been a great growth in the purchase of mutual funds shares, and as a consequence it has become one of the major and interesting aspects of investment stocks. This has had a great effect upon the life insurance business. As a matter of fact, quite recently the contest between companies became such that it was obvious that some kind of solution had to be found. One of the solutions was that the insurance companies moved into the fund field, and the investment funds companies are now moving into the insurance business. On the surface the solution apparently related to a balanced program so that almost any consumer in a particular area could be fitted out with something that was suited to him.
I have no quarrel with this particular point of view, and this point has nothing to do with what may be one of the abuses in this field; that is the so-called load factor of many of these mutual funds, and I refer to the charge which runs from 7 to 9 per cent at the sales end. After all, mutual fund shares are peculiar kinds of shares. They are shares that you ordinarily cannot buy at a brokerage office. The whole business exists through a high pressure form of sales campaign, which is unusual in the stock trade. Not even the penny gold stocks had the constant pushing, systematic kind of sales presentation which mutual fund shares have.
As a matter of fact, some of the serious companies in the field grew very concerned about the sales part of the operation. In this regard I should like to quote from the Montreal Gazette of November 1, 1962 under the heading "Regulatory body set up by mutual fund industry". The article reads in part:
The Canadian mutual fund industry has established a self-regulatory association with a charter membership covering more than 98 per cent of the $750 million-plus of industry assets of funds eligible for membership.
The new association-The Canadian Mutual Funds Association-is intended "to encourage adherence to high ethical standards by all elements of the mutual funds industry."
I assume, I think with some justice, that this self-regulatory organization was formed to intercept what might have been legal actions taken by provincial and perhaps federal governments, particularly because of the operation of these sales forces. It was not that sales aspect I particularly wanted to deal with today, although the high sales pressure and the tremendous growth of the mutual funds industry ties in with the point I wish to make.
If any hon. Members wish to look at the 1964 survey of investment funds, produced by the Financial Post, they will see that it lists all the Canadian investment funds. This is most useful information because it describes or gives a synopsis of the management of each of the funds, and in almost every case sets out the management fee. This is what this bill is really related to-the management fee and the cost of this management fee to a person who is buying or holding mutual funds.
Taking one of the larger Canadian organizations as an example, Investors Mutual, and the constellation of companies around it-the advisory company, Investors Syndicate, and some of the other groups or parts of groups that are contained in it, such as Investors Trust Company and Investors International Mutual Fund Limited-one can see that the standard fee is usually one eighth of 1 per cent of the net assets taken quarterly, which works out roughly to one half of 1 per cent of the net assets as the management fee. That may not seem like very much, but when these funds reach the stage where they involve a $400 million, $500 million, or a billion dollar market, you can see that this is a tremendously important form of revenue for whoever it is who controls the management establishment.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Since the high sales force keeps pushing the number of shares that are on the market or that are out in people's hands, and since this increase has been taking place in a rising market recently, this one eighth of 1 per cent determined quarterly has been immensely profitable. You are not talking about something that involves a few thousand dollars in terms of investment advice or managerial advice. In the case of Investors Mutual and the substantial set of companies collected around it, you are talking of sums ranging from $5 million to $15 million or $16 million. This is a very considerable percentage. Management costs, as worked out on

the average in this Financial Post survey, are somewhere around 5 per cent, and that does not include the sales load which is a responsibility within the actual purchase and runs to about 8 per cent.
A considerable percentage of management cost is taken up, of course, by boards of directors fees, arrangements for meetings and, I suppose, legal fees and this kind of thing. If anyone has looked at the section on Investors Mutual of Canada he will see that the actual management costs relate to two legal fees, custodian's fees, management fees, directors' fees and so on, but the main burden is the management fee.

The amazing thing about these mutual funds-this holds true in Canada-is that in the main the very same people tend to be in control and tend to be directors of both the mutual fund and also of the management company that gives management advice. In other words, as is made very clear in Mr. Smith's book, they really cannot lose. The argument, as Mr. Smith puts it on page 18, is:
Mutual funds are in the business of investing, and are experts at it. No amateur can, or should, try to do in his spare time what the mutual funds are doing full time. The mutual fund puts expert advice and full time management at the disposal of even the most modest investor. Implicit in this argument is the promise of greater profits-a porfolio managed by experts does better than one that has no such management. Otherwise there is no need for experts.
This is the great argument in connection with this matter. But here you come to the fact that the managers who give this management advice are in most cases exactly the same people as are on the boards of directors of the funds themselves. This is a pretty nice business if you are able to take your advantages as a director and man-

ager of a fund and also to take your cut as an advisor, and one of the elements in this is that in essence you cannot lose. You are on a fixed kind of ratio. In the case of Investors Mutual and the companies around it the interesting thing is that, whereas the main fund is a very large one and some of its more recent companies are still at a much lower level, the percentage of the take is the same. Obviously the solution to this kind of thing from the point of view of the person who buys mutual shares is to have incorporated in the Companies Act or in the trust deeds of these companies some kind of sliding scale, because obviously there is not that great an increase in difficulty in managing or investing or giving investment advice as the thing goes up in terms of the kind of percentage that is on a flat rate basis. Obviously someone like Mr. Fullerton, who advised the Canada Council with regard to its investments, is the kind of person who would be advising a company such as Investors Mutual.
The whole point of the case is that there is no real argument that as the fund increases in size it becomes tremendously more difficult to handle. As a matter of fact, in the main the arguments are that basically it becomes easier. I am especially concerned about this matter and I again take the Investors Group as an example, because they are Canadian companies which are subsidiaries of very large American companies and there are, of course, interlocking directorships and management and advisory services. In other words, the people who are providing the management in Canada in this particular case, the Investors Syndicate operation-this is set out on page 18 of the 1962 annual report of Investors Mutual- are doing extremely well out of the advising and managing.
From what I have been able to discover a private Member cannot really bring in an effective bill to set up some kind of sliding scale for management fees, but one of the ways to do it is to introduce a penalty under the Criminal Code, which by its punitive threat will force a split between the advisory group and the actual group that has the fund. In other words, it would force a separation and make the fund group resort to some kind of contract with people other than themselves, which it seems to me is sensible. In order to achieve this, and I am coming now to the title of the bill, it was necessary to provide for something under
May 21, 1965

the Criminal Code to forbid this practice, and this is what the new section 325A set out in the bill tries to do. The reference to the Judas-Tree simply represents the use of a somewhat fancy name to cover the situation that the bill would create if it were passed. Under this new section of the Criminal Code any person would hang himself if he were in the position of being both the adviser and the advised and was able to take benefit from both roles. The Biblical connection, I suppose, is the fact that there is supposedly a kind of tree which bears red flowers, I believe, that represent blood, on which tree Judas is supposed to have hanged himself after taking money for, in a sense, a betrayal of interest.
The hon. Member who asked the question wanted a translation of the explanatory notes. I think this is uncalled for, particularly from him. I look upon him, Mr. Speaker, as the William Jennings Bryan of the Ottawa Valley. I can imagine the hon. gentleman giving the Cross of Gold speech in this House, and these references that align him with that great emancipator are surely an indication that he knows. He is just guying me; he is just kidding me. He knows what these explanatory notes mean, and if he has the opportunity to speak in this debate, which I am sure he will take if he can, I think he will reveal his very clear understanding of what these explanatory notes mean.
I only have a couple of minutes left and I want to touch on one warning which in a sense is partly to myself. I am under no illusions that it is the business of a private Member of Parliament to knock down what has become a very large and important business, as a matter of fact a particular kind of business in which I have put a few dollars myself. But I think it is incumbent upon all of us who are interested in the investment and securities field, which touches so many people, to take a very close look at the situation to see that the investor is getting the best possible break.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I suggest to you when you have a situation where the great majority of the mutual funds in this country, these open end funds with their heavy sales load of around 8 per cent, which is made necessary because of the high pressure work that is involved in selling because of our social and economic strata, and at the same time they have this fixed management fee which bears no relationship to the difficulty or scope of the work, and 22620-103
Criminal Code
when you consider that we are very well provided in this country with brokers and investment analysis groups, when we have an almost staggeringly large number of periodicals providing information in this field, then this amendment is necessary. I do not believe any country has such a group of private stockbrokers and investment analysts as we seem to have gathered, particularly around business circles in Montreal and Toronto. It would seem to me there is no excuse for any of these funds retaining or having a connection with a management group that is captive, or to be the captive of any particular management group. I am thinking of a management group that manages in an advisory sense of how to place, how to time or how to select your investments.
I feel, therefore, that the purpose at least if not the way it is approached in this bill is a very worth-while one. I feel it is one which should appeal to Members generally.
I think the point itself is at least worthy of consideration by a committee of this House, and I am thinking more of the Banking and Commerce Committee. It seems to me that in one or two sessions such a committee could quickly ascertain whether or not there is anything to what I suspect, not a sort of plundering or raid, really not tremendous corruption, but an overcharge, if you want, a possibility of particularly more abuse as these funds expand that affects and hurts the ordinary person who invests in this field.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the question of whether or not a bill such as this is referred to a committee depends, I realize, upon the decision of the Government spokesman, whatever may be said pro or con. I do not know whether it will be pro or con on this occasion. Despite the humour and the embarrassment in which I found myself last year when I discussed this bill, and Lord knows I have never been in a more embarrassing situation in parliament than on that particular occasion, I am serious about the purpose of this bill. I would not like anyone to carry on from the slapstick that my own misadventure and inadequacy created last session. I hope that the purpose will be taken seriously by someone on the Ministerial benches, and that the Government will look at the idea to see whether or not it at least merits consideration by one of the committees of this House.

How can we, with our limited powers under our constitution, legislate to protect the investor either by way of disclosure or by way of regulation? A short time ago I was very interested to see an address by Bora Laskin of the University of Toronto law school, in which he indicted legislators, and I think with justification, for not having the courage or the drive to take hold of new areas of legislation and to move forward constitutionally by grasping the nettle in these areas where apparently at first sight the question of jurisdiction is a difficult one.
I think, as in so many areas, we in this country have been far too diffident in accepting challenges and needs for legislation, and we have avoided them on the question of the doubtful constitutionality in these areas where legislation is so badly needed.
I might point out that emanating from the decisions in the anti-trust cases in the United States, where quite obviously in its inception the constitution was drawn with far less federal powers than were given to us in the British North America Act, they have been able at the federal level, under the aegis of their S.E.C. legislation, to give far more adequate protection to the private investor in the public corporate field than we have been able to do, or have attempted to do.
I think it should be a mark of some considerable concern to us Canadians when we see a situation such as occurred with Texas Gulf Sulphur, where not too long ago insiders with confidential information apparently took advantage of this position to make considerable fortunes on the Canadian and American stock exchanges by virtue of that inside information. The source of new wealth which led to this situation was situated here in Canada, in Timmins, and yet nothing was done. Apparently there was not even any public concern or investigation at the Canadian level, and the remedial action had to be taken in Washington. Surely to goodness that is something that should trouble us all, because this involves a situation with an investment the wealth of which is based on Canadian natural resources. But we apparently can give no protection to the investor, and we have to look to Washington to do so in the case where stock is also listed on the American stock exchange.
Again, I think if anyone is responsible in this area and must carry the burden, it is the Liberal Party in this country. The party of which the hon. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) is a member, to my knowledge and at latest review, although they change quite 22620-1031
often, was still a Socialist Party when last heard from. If such be the case then I do not think this area, the area of public corporate investment and the protection of private investors, should be of great concern to them, because if they are true to their principles in the Regina Manifesto-

speechtext: I wonder if I could ask the hon. Member a question. I could raise a point of order, as I thought he might be straying, but if you take the other side of the coin, does this mean hon. Members of the Liberal Party have no business speaking about, or advocating the Canada Development Corporation which, as the hon. Member knows, has been labelled by quite a number of people, including the President of the Montreal stock exchange, as some form of wrong-headed Socialism?

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTEREST-MUTUAL TRUST ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, with respect, I think that the hon. Member has every right to discuss these matters, just as we have to discuss the Canada Development Corporation, but I do think it is the primary responsibility-and that is the point I am trying to make-of the Liberal Party, which professes by definition to have a philosophy founded on private enterprise, to see to it that that private enterprise and the public corporation approach to investment is made a fair and honest aboveboard game, in which the small investor can be protected.
We have often heard criticism that the political parties in our country are too much alike, that no one can tell the players without a program because everybody is just the same. I think this is one area in which possibly the philosophy of the Conservative Party and that of the Liberal Party could quite well be different. The Conservative Party, if it some day returns to Conservatism, will probably take a position which would be for less interference than the Liberal Party could well espouse in questions affecting public corporations and investments.
I suggest that in this country we should be concerned with the very grave situation that the hon. Member has brought to the attention of the House, the protection of mutual fund investors. Is it proper that the purchaser of mutual funds, who is buying by small weekly payments, should be gouged for an 8 per cent commission on the purchase of each unit of shares that he buys?
Should there be some protection in that area for the public investor? Again, usually the purchaser of mutual funds is not a sophisticated stock market operator. As the hon..

May 21, 1965
Criminal Code
Member points out, quite often the mutuals are sold from door to door by salesmen who are not well informed on the various aspects of the field. Is this not a proper area for legislation, to see to it that the purchaser is protected, and to see to it that full disclosure in every aspect is made to the potential purchaser?
I think most of us agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) who is much concerned to see the buying back of our economy by Canadians. I can think of nothing which would have a more salutary effect in that direction than if the small investor were assured under our legislation that he is getting the best possible dollar value for his money, that his dollar of investment is not being watered down, that he is given that protection by government legislation.
Again in these mutual funds with interlocking directorships, to the best of my knowledge there is no legislation which makes it mandatory, upon at least a quarterly basis, to indicate to each investor what stocks have been purchased and sold, and at what price they were purchased and sold in each quarter of the year. Nor is there any regulation which makes it mandatory to indicate to investors at what price stock they hold in their portfolios was purchased. Again to the best of my knowledge, with interlocking directorships there is nothing which protects the investor in this situation.
Let us say the director of the mutual fund has also an interest in company A, and maybe company A is not doing too well, and on the stock market they are a little worried about maintaining the price of their stock.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
He is a director of the mutual fund. What is to prevent his advocating the purchase of the stock in company A to help company A, not the mutual fund? These are areas of conflict which need investigation and legislation. I do not think we on this side should avoid our constitutional responsibility in this regard. Undoubtedly provincial co-operation must be sought in this area. The workings of stock exchanges are clearly a provincial responsibility under our constitution, I am sure the provinces in their wisdom are just as concerned about this problem as we are.
Is it not a striking example of how little protection we give to individuals in this country when a company such as International Nickel, along with other United States corporations, whose wealth is derived entirely from Canadian natural resources must

give more information to its American stockholders than to its Canadian stockholders? The company provides two annual reports. One of them tells virtually nothing; it is prepared for the Canadian stockholders. The other, for the benefit of United States stockholders, gives particulars of any benefits or emoluments given to directors, such as pension funds, going into the greatest possible detail, as required by the regulations, for the benefit of U.S. shareholders. This is an area of great concern to those of us who believe in the importance of our people buying back control of their economy.
If the investor knows he will be protected by the Government-that he is not being milked by the boys on the inside, he will be much more prone to invest in equities and play a part, however humble, in the buying back of the Canadian economy. But when every day he sees stories such as ti\e one describing the take-over of Canadian oil companies last year, where insiders made a fabulous profit at the expense of private investors who had no privity to inside information, he is not encouraged to invest in equities. If we are to have a wider and broader base for equity holdings-and these are in my opinion, the best kind of base for a capital structure in a private enterprise economy-we must see to it that the investor is protected to a far greater degree than is now the case. I commend the hon. Member for bringing this small facet of unfairness to the attention of the House.

It is surely a function of government under a private enterprise system to see to it that the system works for the greatest advantage of all. In a wider area, I think this subject should be subsumed in a broader study of means by which the consumer can be protected. We are remiss in permitting the private enterprise system to

I had the pleasure of being in the House on a previous occasion when this bill was brought down. I remember the merriment at that time, some of it at the expense of the hon. Member for Port Arthur. It was all done in the best of humour and at the end of the day I think the hon. Member enjoyed it as much as we did.
I should like to turn to the explanatory notes. Previous speakers have referred to them, but so far no one has put them on record in Hansard during the course of this debate. There has been so much reference to them that I think it would be wrong of me to ignore this opportunity to put into the record the pulsing prose which appears in these explanatory notes. They read as follows:
For the Janusary of Mammon who has everything; for the con-man confiscador of Bay Street boardroom; for the investment double-I dealer in cosa nostrums, surecurities, salves gui-peut and pink pep pills for the anaemic income ills of widow and pensioner, this Bill provides a Judas-Tree.
I can well imagine the difficulty which faces even a man with the capabilities of the hon. Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) in interpreting this paragraph. When we referred to it on the last occasion the bill was before us I had a feeling that the hon. Member for Port Arthur had not written it at all -that it was possibly some of the 19th century prose of his hon. friend the Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). I asked him one day on the aircraft between here and Vancouver who had written

it-I had become curious; it had become a research project of mine. He denied my theory. He said he had not written it. Actually he said that piece was written by the hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge).
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I subscribe to another theory. I certainly do not believe the hon. Member for Port Arthur wrote it because he is a capable journalist and would use the blue pencil if he caught a piece of copy of that kind. I think it was written by the author of "The Grim Truth about Mutual Funds", Mr. Ralph Lee Smith, around whom this bill is written.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this bill is really not a bill so much as a book review. It was written as a result of a book which the hon. Member for Port Arthur read, and to which he referred both today and in his remarks last year. At that time he said, as reported at page 8958 of Hansard for October 9, 1964:
It is rather obvious, particularly if you have read the book "The Grim Truth about Mutual Funds by Ralph Lee Smith, that this practice has caused serious concern in the securities and exchange commission of the United States.
Then he went on to quote some paragraphs from the works of Mr. Ralph Lee Smith on the subject. So it is today that the reviews of this book are indeed, following the passage of a couple of years and the presentation of this bill on two separate occasions in the House, becoming lengthier than the book itself.
I do not take quite the same view as that taken by the hon. Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) on the matter of regulation. Certainly there should be no regulation by the House of Commons, because I believe that the regulation of securities falls rather within the jurisdiction of the provinces than within the jurisdiction of the Federal Government. I do not take the attitude that this House should involve itself to the extent of attempting to regulate mutual funds. The discussions we have had in this chamber during private Members' hours tend to show to provincial legislatures and to the country the need for regulation in some of these areas; but I would be happy to see the provinces, which constitutionally should look after this matter-being charged with controlling the securities market-enter into the field of regulating mutual funds if, indeed, mutual funds need to be regulated to the extent the hon. Member suggested.

He said there were a great many of them and, indeed, there are a great many mutual funds for sale today. I detected in his remarks a note of alarm at the fact that there should be so many salesmen abroad selling mutual funds and that there should be a large number of mutual funds available for public purchase.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTEREST-MUTUAL TRUST ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I correct the impression which I gave. I wonder whether the hon. Member would accept that I am not alarmed by the number of salesmen or the number of funds. I am alarmed by the lack of information and understanding on the part of many people who buy them. I still believe in the old credo of beware of the seller; but if the buyer knows very little about the situation, then I think it is up to public agencies or, as the hon. Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) suggested, for the Liberal Party itself, to get involved in the information, the education, and if you want the penalizing process.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTEREST-MUTUAL TRUST ORGANIZATIONS

Mr. Speaker, I accept the hon. Member's explanation. I am sure it must become difficult for salesmen of any stock or of mutual funds, or indeed of insurance, to have any great knowledge about the particular company which owns the stock or in regard to its worth. It is often very difficult for the small investor, the small purchaser of insurance, to know the details and to be able to assess the value of a particular stock or of a particular mutual fund. I think it must be the trust of the individual, of the person from whom he makes his purchase, that for him makes it worth while to enter into the particular investment.
For my own part, if I were going to buy a mutual fund today I think I would want to talk to some of those competent investors in the market who would be able to give me their opinions regarding a particular mutual fund. I would want to discuss the matter with my banker and have a talk with him about what were his feelings regarding the purchase of a mutual fund. I think every
small investor today who has money to invest in securities and in equities and is anxious to put money into a growing industrial Canada tends to follow exactly those same lines, and it seems to me that investors should follow those lines. Canadians are widely known for their caution in banking affairs and in placing their money into insurance, so there is an inherent caution among Canadians in making investments of this kind. It should certainly be a warning to Canadians, who have read articles in the papers of recent days about some stock market transactions which recently took place in Ontario, to follow such practice and consult those competent in the field before their savings of a lifetime, money they have earned through hard labour, are put into investments of a dubious nature at the invitation of people of whom they have no knowledge and who themselves seem incapable of imparting accurate information in regard to the subject.
